newsitem.title: SPAIN: "Dirty war" ruling may dog Spain's Gonzalez.
newsitem.headline: "Dirty war" ruling may dog Spain's Gonzalez.

text.p: Spanish Supreme Court judges voted six to four on Tuesday against questioning former prime minister Felipe Gonzalez about a 1980s "dirty war" on Basque rebels -- a split ruling which could dog him for the rest of his life.
"Obviously this doesn't absolve Gonzalez politically, nor does it absolve him judicially," said Jose Luis Galan, lawyer for the victims' families. "He now becomes the eternal suspect."

After six hours of closed-doors debate in the top tribunal's second chamber, which deals with members of parliament like Gonzalez, Justice Jose Augusto de Vega told reporters early on Tuesday six judges had voted against questioning him.
The fact that the other four had cast dissenting votes was seized upon by the Socialist leader's foes as evidence of a strong case for calling him, had he been a common citizen.
State prosecutors also made a point of warning that they may reverse their advice not to quiz him if new evidence emerges.
"People might perhaps think this is the end of the trial...that isn't so," Attorney-General Juan Ortiz Urculo told a radio interviewer.

Gonzalez, who lost elections in March after 13 years in power, denies charges by former security chiefs and disgruntled fellow Socialists that he knew of the 1983-87 campaign of bombings, kidnappings, torture and murders by members of the security forces and hired gunmen that killed 28 people.

Despite the "dirty war" scandal and a long string of Socialist corruption cases, he remains hugely popular and even has a small edge in opinion polls now over Jose Maria Aznar, his conservative victor in the March elections.
Because he will not be questioned for now, Gonzalez does not risk going to jail -- but neither can he have his name cleared for good, should he be questioned and found innocent.
Friends and foes agreed the high-profile split in the Supreme Court would leave him vulnerable to permanent suspicion.
Alfredo Perez Rubalcaba, a close aide who was his chief of staff until their fall from power, said he was glad Gonzalez would not be called but admitted that the debate may never end.
"You can be assured that in light of the political connotations of the case...well, there are people for whom the matter will never be closed," he told a radio interviewer.

Technically, the 10 judges were deciding not on the entire "dirty war" but only on an appeal about whether the Socialist leader should be questioned in the chief case in the covert campaign -- the mistaken-identity kidnapping in December 1983 of Basque businessman Segundo Marey.
Also safe from questioning together with Gonzalez are his former deputy Narcis Serra and Socialist leader Jose Maria Benegas, both of whom were included in Tuesday's decision.

The only new accusations against Gonzalez since a similar ruling by the Supreme Court's investigating justice in April have come from Luis Roldan, a former Socialist head of the paramilitary Civil Guard who is himself accused of fraud and embezzlement while in office.
He has testified that the operations against presumed rebels from ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) were official government policy and that Gonzalez was fully involved.

Gonzalez's first interior minister, Jose Barrionuevo, is already on trial at the Supreme Court on charges of masterminding and funding the shadowy death squads known as the GAL (the Spanish initials for Anti-terrorist Liberation Groups).
